newsitem.title: USA: U.S. daughters' day touches UN, White House, Congress.
newsitem.headline: U.S. daughters' day touches UN, White House, Congress.

text.p: America's daughters -- and some sons -- went to steel mills, offices, nursing homes, the United Nations, Congress and the White House on Thursday for "Take Our Daughters To Work Day."

For the fifth year, the feminist event urged workers to bring their daughters or other girls aged 9-15 to see the world of work and promote their ambition and self-esteem. Critics have complained boys were excluded, so some offices had co-ed events.
President Bill Clinton gave the day his approval in a White House statement.

"We dedicate this special day each year to empowering girls with the encouragement and practical work experiences that will enable them to become leaders in the workplace of the future," Clinton said. "Young girls must never believe that there are limitations on what they can do or become in this country."
On Capitol Hill, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said his daughter was at work in Jackson, Mississippi, but had to pay too much in taxes "which I don't think the law intended."

Among Democrats, Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota brought his daughter, Lindsay, a high school junior, to a news conference, and said the congressional vote on a chemical weapons treaty would affect her generation.
Lindsay Daschle told reporters the day with her father might "give me some background for a future career." Did she want to be a senator? "Maybe."

At United Nations headquarters in New York, about 600 girls came to work, starting the day by listening to a welcoming speech by Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who patiently answered questions on how he spent his day.

New York law firm Weil, Gotshal and Manges staged a mock trial for young visitors to determine if Dorothy killed the Wicked Witch of the West in "The Wizard of Oz" and whether it was justifiable homicide.
In Miami, the Coast Guard took about 25 girls and a few boys for a boat trip around Biscayne Bay. Although the Coast Guard is predominantly male, some women were on duty during the visit.
"It was great for the girls to see women in different, non-traditional roles, like a mechanic. The coxswain was a woman too," said Lieutenant Virginia Elcesser.
In Massachusetts, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers put dozens of children to work for part of the day, and then sent the youngsters on a nature walk with their sponsors.
The day is a programme of the Ms Foundation for Women, which acknowledged criticism over the exclusion of boys.

"Because girls experience distress at adolescence, the Ms. Foundation for Women has designed Take Our Daughters to Work Day as a positive intervention at that time," the foundation said in a statement. "... boys deserve programmes and services that address their unique needs and concerns, which to be most effective would occur during early childhood."
